name: THE HOT BUN IN THE SUMMER-THYME BURGER

recipe.history:
Thyme is one of the foundational herbs of the Mediterranean world, a low-growing perennial of the genus Thymus that has carpeted the rocky hillsides of southern France, Spain, Greece, and North Africa for millennia. Ancient Egyptians used thyme in the embalming process; ancient Greeks burned it as incense in temples, believing its smoke conveyed courage — indeed, the word thyme may derive from the Greek thymos, meaning spirit or courage. Romans planted it across Europe as they expanded their empire, and it naturalized readily in the thin soils of Provence, the garrigues of Languedoc, and the slopes of the Pyrenees, where it grows wild and pungent in the summer heat. Lemon thyme, a specific cultivar with a pronounced citrus character from its high thymol and carvacrol content alongside lemony terpenes, became a favorite of French and Italian cooks for its ability to brighten rather than simply season — it lifts the flavors around it rather than dominating them.

Thyme arrived in the American herb garden via French and British colonial cooking traditions, and it has always been a workhorse of the American kitchen — standard in stuffings, roasts, and stews. Its use in a summer burger context reflects the California and New American cooking movements of the 1980s and 1990s, when chefs began treating herbs not as background notes but as primary flavor voices. Lemon thyme aioli, grilled zucchini seasoned with thyme, and a thyme-scented brioche bun all express the same herb in three different registers simultaneously: raw and bright in the aioli, smoky and caramelized with the zucchini, and warm and faintly floral baked into the bun. This layered approach to a single ingredient — using it differently in each component — is the technique that separates composed cooking from mere assembly.

Summer means thyme to me in a way that is almost Proustian. I grew up visiting a relative who kept an herb garden in a raised bed along the south-facing wall of her house, and by July the thyme was always enormous, spilling over the edges of the bed in cascading branches. She used it in everything during those months — tucked under chicken skin, thrown into grilling marinades, bruised and steeped in lemonade. I learned to cook with thyme partly by watching her and partly by the smell of those summer kitchens, which is why I put it in the bun itself on this burger: the moment the thyme-scented brioche goes into the oven, the whole kitchen smells like those July afternoons, and for a moment the season feels permanent.

Cooking a burger to medium rare — 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit — is particularly important with this recipe because the brightness and lift of the lemon thyme aioli and the grilled zucchini need the richness and yielding texture of medium-rare beef to anchor them. These are light, summery flavors, and they would be overwhelmed by the dry, heavy texture of overcooked meat in a way that heavier toppings — cheese sauces, onion jams — might compensate for. The pink, moist interior of a medium-rare patty provides both textural contrast and a reservoir of rendered fat that enriches every bite. A well-done patty on this burger would taste like summer squash and aioli on cardboard. Medium rare is the only preparation that keeps all the elements in balance.
ingredients: 3 large eggs plus 1 for egg wash
2 tbsp fresh lemon thyme leaves, finely chopped
2 tsp fresh lemon thyme leaves, minced
1 clove garlic, minced to paste with salt
Fine sea salt and white pepper
3 medium zucchini, sliced lengthwise into 1/4-inch planks
Fine sea salt and black pepper
1/2 cup sun-dried tomatoes in oil, drained and roughly chopped
instructions: 1. Make the thyme brioche buns: Bloom yeast in warm milk 5 minutes. Combine flour, sugar, and salt in a stand mixer. Add yeast mixture and 3 eggs; knead with dough hook 8 minutes on medium. Add softened butter one tablespoon at a time, kneading between additions. Add lemon thyme leaves and zest. Knead 5 more minutes until incorporated and smooth. Cover; refrigerate overnight.
2. Divide dough into 6 equal balls. Proof on parchment-lined sheet at room temperature 2.5–3 hours. Brush with egg wash. Bake at 375°F for 16–18 minutes until golden. Cool on a rack.

3. Make the lemon thyme aioli: Whisk egg yolks and Dijon together. Drizzle in mixed oils very slowly, whisking constantly, until thick and emulsified. Whisk in lemon juice, zest, thyme, and garlic paste. Season with salt and white pepper. Refrigerate.
4. Marinate the zucchini: Combine olive oil, thyme sprigs, smashed garlic, red pepper flakes, salt, and pepper. Add zucchini planks and toss. Marinate 20 minutes.

5. Form the patties: Combine ground chuck with salt, pepper, and fresh thyme leaves. Divide into 4 portions (about 8 oz each). Shape into 4.5-inch patties with a center dimple. Refrigerate 20 minutes.

6. Heat a grill or grill pan to high heat. Grill zucchini planks 2–3 minutes per side until charred grill marks form and flesh is tender. Set aside. Grill lemon halves cut-side down 3 minutes until caramelized.

7. On the same grill or a hot cast-iron skillet, cook patties undisturbed 3–4 minutes. Flip; crumble goat cheese over each patty. Cover loosely. Cook 2–3 more minutes. Target internal temperature 130–135°F for medium rare. Remove and rest, tented in foil, for 3 minutes.
8. Toast brioche buns cut-side down in butter in a skillet over medium heat until golden, about 90 seconds.

9. Assemble: Spread lemon thyme aioli on both bun halves. Layer baby greens on the bottom bun. Top with grilled zucchini planks. Place the goat-cheese-topped patty. Add sun-dried tomatoes. Squeeze a bit of grilled lemon over the top. Finish with flaky sea salt. Crown with the top bun.
